Start by defining your roles: who you are for others and for yourself.
Put the big rocks in first: set 1–2 goals for each role and schedule them into days.
Hold a task to drag it into another quadrant. Quadrant II is where effectiveness lives.
Quadrant I: crises and deadlines. Do it as soon as possible.
Quadrant II: growth, relationships, planning. This is where effectiveness is born.
Quadrant III: other people\'s priorities and interruptions. Delegate or cut down.
Quadrant IV: time wasters. Is it worth doing at all?
Check off each day. Small daily steps are how you sharpen the saw.

resources.string: Write down who you want to be and what matters most to you.
“Begin with the end in mind.” A personal mission statement is your constitution: the principles, values and character you choose. Check every decision and weekly plan against it.

• How do I want to be remembered?
• Which values matter most to me?
• Who do I want to be in each of my roles?
• What would I do if I could not fail?
Roles are the areas of your life: partner, parent, friend, professional, leader. Give each one weekly and long-term goals so that no important area is left without attention.

Renewing yourself in four dimensions: physical, mental, social-emotional and spiritual.
Between stimulus and response there is a space to choose. You are responsible for your choices. Focus on your circle of influence, the things you can change, rather than your circle of concern.
Begin with the end in mind
Picture who you want to become and write a personal mission statement. It becomes the compass for every role, goal and daily decision.
Manage yourself, not time. Plan your week by roles, put the big rocks in first and spend more time in Quadrant II: important but not urgent.
Look for solutions that benefit everyone. Effective relationships are built on trust and mutual benefit, not competition.
Seek first to understand, then to be understood
Listen with the intent to understand, not to reply. Empathic listening opens the way to real understanding.
Value differences. Together, people can create solutions better than any one of them would find alone.
Renew yourself regularly: physically, mentally, socially-emotionally and spiritually. This is the habit that sustains all the others.

1. Write your personal mission.
2. Define your roles and set weekly goals for each.
3. At the start of the week, spread tasks across the days; keep the unplanned ones under “No date”.
4. Didn't get to something? Just drag the task to another day.
5. Check the matrix: what from Quadrant II can you do today?
6. In the evening, write a few lines in the journal and check off your habits.
